section_1.title: Prerequisites: The Language of Vectors
section_1.content: Briefly define a basis as a 'coordinate system' (the grid lines of a vector space). Emphasize that a vector is just a physical displacement, while coordinates are our instructions on how to reach it using basis vectors.
section_1.example: Imagine a vector pointing to a treasure chest. Whether you describe its position using North/East or a rotated 'Map Grid', the treasure chest doesn't move—only the numbers (coordinates) change.

section_2.title: The Problem: Viewing Space from Different Angles
section_2.content: Introduce two different basis sets, B (standard) and C (the 'new' perspective). Explain that a vector 'v' can be represented as [v]B or [v]C. The goal is to find the 'bridge' (Transition Matrix) that maps coordinates from one view to the other.
section_2.example: A cat (the vector) sits on a floor. Camera A (Basis B) sees it at (2, 1). Camera B (Basis C), mounted at a 45-degree angle, sees the same cat at different coordinate values.

section_3.title: Constructing the Transition Matrix
section_3.content: Show the visual process of expressing the 'new' basis vectors as linear combinations of the 'old' basis vectors. These coefficients become the columns of the Transition Matrix P. Visual: Use an animation of grid lines warping from a square to a tilted parallelogram.
section_3.example: If your new basis vectors are v1=(1,1) and v2=(-1,1), place these as columns in matrix P to create the machine that transforms 'New Coordinates' into 'Standard Coordinates'.

section_4.title: The Change of Basis Formula: The Transformation
section_4.content: Formalize the equation: [v]B = P * [v]C. Explain that P is the 'translator'. To go back, we use P-inverse. Visual: A 'Translator Engine' icon where inputting coordinates from Basis C and multiplying by matrix P yields the coordinates in Basis B.
section_4.example: Use a robot character navigating a room. It calculates its movement in its 'local' body-centered frame (Basis C) and uses the Transition Matrix to translate that into the 'global' room coordinates (Basis B).

section_5.title: Summary & Application
section_5.content: Reiterate that we aren't changing the vector, just our 'description' of it. Final visual: A side-by-side comparison of the same vector shifting its coordinate labels as the grid underlying it rotates.
section_5.example: Computer graphics: Rotating a 3D model involves changing the basis of the object's vertices so they align with the camera's perspective.

        self.setup_layout("Prerequisites: The Language of Vectors",

                           "Coordinates depend on the basis chosen."])
        
        # Define base objects
        axes = Axes(x_range=[-2, 3], y_range=[-2, 3], axis_config={"include_tip": True}).scale(0.6)

        coord_label = MathTex("(2, 1.5)", color=YELLOW).next_to(v_label, RIGHT)
